## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Daddarajātaka* (Ja 172) is a canonical Pali Jātaka tale belonging to the *Jātaka* collection. The opening verse begins with the words *Ko nu saddena mahatā* (“Who is it with a mighty cry, etc.”) [Fausböll 1879a]. It should not be confused with another homonymous story in the collection, the *Daddarajātaka* (Ja 304) [Cowell 1897b].

According to the frame story, the Buddha related the tale while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the monk Kokālika [Fausböll 1879a]. In the introductory narrative, Kokālika attempts to display his learning, described as dressing in robes of unusual colors—specifically colors identified with the *kaṇṭakurandaka* and *kaṇikāra* flowers [Spink 2006; Piya Tan 2002]. In the story of the past, a jackal attempts to imitate the roar of lions, thereby shaming young lions into silence [Bodhi 2003]. In the story's identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the jackal as Kokālika in a past life, a young lion (*sīhapotaka*) as Rāhula, and the lion king (*sīharājā*) as the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1879a].
